title: JEPA4R: Embodied JEPA World Models with 4D Point Planning
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models predict future embeddings instead of pixels and plan in latent space. Two challenges remain: 2D images leave the metric geometry that manipulation acts on implicit and entangled with appearance, and what these models imagine stays hidden, as they are mostly judged in simulation by short-horizon latent planning. We present JEPA4R, a JEPA world model that observes single-depth-camera point clouds, predicts and plans in their latent space, and acts through a policy head on its frozen latents; we call this 4D point planning. A decoder on the frozen world model shows what it imagines as 4D point clouds, with a mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 steps. Under the policy-learning protocols of OGBench and CortexBench, JEPA4R leads pixel JEPA models on OGBench Cube-Single, Cube-Double, Cube-Triple and Scene, and ranks first on MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate with 98.4% and 88.0%, above the runner-up, R3M, at 96.0% and 65.3%. Trained only in a digital twin, JEPA4R and its policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm with both a gripper and a dexterous hand.

title: MOBO-CAPS: Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization with Cardinality-Aware Pareto Selection
abstract: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) traditionally aims to approximate the entire Pareto front, but, due to resource constraints, real-world deployment is often limited to testing a small, representative subset of solutions. Hence current methods first approximate the full front before selecting solutions, potentially wasting costly evaluations. We formalize this problem as Multi-objective Bayesian Optimization with Cardinality-aware Pareto Selection (MOBO-CAPS), where the goal is to identify a set of exactly M solutions with high hypervolume. We propose two practical cardinality-aware acquisition strategies: REHVI, a replacement-aware approximation to expected hypervolume improvement, and CHO-UCB, which constructs an optimistic M-point set by optimizing a collective UCB-based hypervolume objective. We prove a sublinear simple regret bound for the batched version of CHO-UCB, and empirically show that cardinality-aware acquisition design improves over standard MOBO followed by post-hoc subset selection across nine benchmarks.

title: Deterministic Bilingual RLHF Preference Calibration and Speech-to-Speech (S2S) Acoustic Prosody Governance: Eliminating Annotator Drift and Boundary Artifacts in South Asian and Global LLM Arena Pipelines
abstract: We formalize VF-RLHF-S2S-2026-007, a deterministic governance and acoustic calibration architecture co-authored by HM Shihabuddin Jashory (ORCID: 0009-0003-4163-0092) and MD Rafiul Islam Shubho (ORCID: 0009-0009-9956-4511) at Vision Flow Research Lab (Vision Flow Group, Wikidata Q141910527). Extending HQAS-8 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23832719) and AMCG-3 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24107586), this technical monograph introduces word-level Whisper boundary alignment, frame-accurate S2S prosody auditing, and deterministic bilingual (bn_BD / en_US) RLHF/SFT preference calibration validated across 1,400+ production evaluation tasks with 98.4% QA rubric precision.

title: KneeFS-Net: A Lightweight Deep Learning Model for Knee Osteoarthritis Severity Assessment with Cross-Domain External Validation
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) grading from radiographs using the Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) scale requires expertise that may be scarce. We present KneeFS-Net, a lightweight ordinal grader (0.8 million parameters; 0.33 GFLOPs) combining spatial, Fourier and state-space features with landmark-guided attention. On the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) test set, KneeFS-Net achieved a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.863, mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.325 and 97.2% within-one-grade accuracy, comparable to models with 9-35-fold more parameters. We evaluated cross-population generalization on two Bangladeshi cohorts, a single-center hospital cohort and a multi-center teleradiology cohort. Without further training or adaptation, the OAI-trained model achieved QWK 0.803, MAE 0.339 and 98.2% within-one-grade accuracy on its hospital cohort, declining to QWK 0.656 and MAE 0.522 on multi-center teleradiology images. Self-supervised pretraining on 6,092 unlabeled radiographs followed by joint fine-tuning achieved QWK 0.823, MAE 0.329 and 99.7% within-one-grade accuracy in cross-validation. These findings demonstrate accurate, efficient KL grading and potential adaptation to new populations with limited annotation.

title: When Zero Is Competitive: A Descriptive Pilot of Transformer and Gate-Graph Surrogates on Random-Angle Quantum Circuits
abstract: We examine supervised classical prediction of all one-qubit Z and two-qubit ZZ expectation values on noiseless, layered 4-10-qubit RX/RY/RZ-CNOT circuits. In a 63-cell stratified workload with disjoint circuit-template tests, we evaluate one transformer encoder and gate-dependency graph neural networks against literal-zero and training-derived constant predictors. On the Arm K training labels, 44.89% of scalar targets have absolute magnitude below 0.05. The held-out-template zero predictor has equal-instance mean absolute error 0.193399, and none of the evaluated transformer checkpoints or final graph-network endpoints achieves a lower score. A separate product-state positive control achieves MAE 0.007755 versus 0.514811 for zero, but does not explain the failure on the entangled workload. The difference between zero and a training-fitted mean constant under training MSE is only 0.14%, a descriptive point estimate without uncertainty analysis. The transformer's 815,233-parameter source identity is locally verified; detailed packed-input semantics have not been independently audited. These results constitute a descriptive pilot, not a causal explanation, formal equivalence test, or impossibility claim. Comparable circuits can be regenerated from the workload specification, but exact frozen datasets and model-run evidence remain private.

title: An Author-Level Component of Clinical Note Length in MIMIC-III Resident Progress Notes: A Testable Hypothesis for Clinical Natural Language Processing
abstract: Background: Clinical natural language processing (NLP) treats notes as records of the patient, but notes are also written by individual clinicians whose habits may shape the text. Objectives: To test, using note length, whether clinical text carries an author-level component after accounting for principal diagnosis. Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study analyzed 62,682 resident progress notes by 435 physicians in the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III (MIMIC-III), a de-identified single-center critical care database (Boston, 2001 to 2012). Study 1 related word count to a fixed 54-term content proxy, overall and at constant proxy value. Study 2 retained notes from the ten most frequent principal diagnoses (20,581 notes; 266 physicians), centered word count on diagnosis means, and estimated the author intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), with and without an admission component. Results: Word count correlated with concept count (r = 0.695; 95% CI 0.680 to 0.710). At constant concept count (11; n = 5,999), the 90th-to-10th percentile length ratio was 1.93. After diagnosis centering, the pooled ICC was 0.225 (95% CI 0.189 to 0.257). With admission modeled, the author share was 0.187 and the admission share 0.244; retaining one random note per author-admission gave 0.201. Physicians at the 10th and 90th percentiles differed by 334 words per note. Conclusions: The content proxy accounted for approximately half the variance in note length, and resident note length clustered measurably by author after accounting for principal diagnosis, including when repeated notes within admissions were modeled. Care-unit conventions, calendar period, and case mix cannot be excluded. Whether this author component affects models trained or evaluated on clinical notes was not tested; we outline three pathways by which it could, with a test for each, and propose author-aware reporting items.

title: Autonomous Multi-modal Agents for ITOps Observability
abstract: ITOps observability products must integrate data from different tools and systems. We present ITOps Observability Studio, a multi-modal multi-agent system that orchestrates observability workflows through collaborative AI agents. Its three-tier architecture features inter-agent communication, specialized LLM-powered agents for data access, schema operations and visualization, and unified tool integration. The system supports natural language to GraphQL translation, GraphQL schema generation, schema mapping, trace data lifecycle management and multi-tool workflows for reliability engineering. Its agents are instrumented with agent analytics, so that their model and tool calls can be traced. We evaluate each agent on its own benchmark, scored against gold answers where they exist and by a model judge for schema mapping and chart quality. Query generation on a public benchmark and routing work well with a current open model, and the data lifecycle management agent solves most of its scenarios. The evaluation exposed defects that only appear when prompts, parsers and serving stacks are tested together, and we report them together with their fixes.

title: Morphology-Decoupled Segmentation for Multiple Tunnel Defects Under Complex Environments
abstract: Automated tunnel-lining inspection must segment different defect geometries: cracks are thin, elongated, and connectivity-sensitive, whereas leakage, lining falling off, and segment damage are spatially extensive and context-dependent. Existing approaches generally apply a common decoder across defect classes or introduce boundary, topology, and directional mechanisms as isolated enhancements. This paper introduces Morphology-Decoupled Segmentation (MDS), in which defect morphology becomes the organising principle for feature routing, decoding, and interaction. A supervised routing module partitions multiscale encoder features into complementary linear and areal streams. The linear stream employs Deformable Strip Attention with image-conditioned direction hypotheses to preserve crack continuity without assuming fixed horizontal or vertical orientations, while the areal stream combines Pyramid Pooling with feature-pyramid fusion to capture diffuse boundaries and regional context. The representations are coupled through gated cross-morphology attention, allowing complementary information exchange while retaining morphology-specific features. A resolution-adaptive tiling and probability-blending pipeline preserves fine defects across variable-resolution imagery. MDS achieves 81.17% mIoU on the internal validation set and improves foreground image-level recognition over a backbone-matched SegDINO model, primarily for areal defects. Controlled ablations demonstrate the complementary contributions of routing supervision and cross-stream interaction while revealing a trade-off between areal-class performance and crack specialisation. The submitted model achieved 67.55% mIoU on an organiser-controlled hidden test, and the team placed second. Selective dynamic INT8 quantisation reduced model storage by 2.83 times with negligible accuracy loss.

title: Practice Is Not Free: Measuring the Embodied Cost of Reset-Free Robot Practice
abstract: When a robot practices without human resets, every attempt still costs wall-clock time, actuator wear, and sometimes a person's attention, yet the schedulers that decide what to practice next treat attempts as free. We present an open, low-cost testbed for measuring these costs: a self-built SO-101 arm runs two demonstration-trained ACT policies that reset each other, with a vision-based success detector and a ledger that records the time, joint travel, and human interventions of every attempt. We formulate cost-aware practice scheduling, in which task selection is rewarded by measured competence gain net of embodied cost, and specify in advance the comparison that will test it. Its first two conditions, run on hardware for 51 minutes of robot time, show that a fixed retry limit did not reduce the share of execution time lost to failures (36%, against 27% for a feasibility rule; not significant) and saved no robot time. The logs suggest why: failures showed no sign of clustering, so a retry right after a failure was as likely to succeed as any other attempt. The ledger also shows that most of the retry rule's extra human time came from cubes knocked out of reach rather than from the rule itself, and a cost-aware rule replayed on the logs recovers the sensible choice without a hand-set limit. title: CreaTrace: Video Creative Plagiarism Detection and Evidence Tracing
abstract: Video creative plagiarism refers to the unauthorized reproduction of creative ideas across videos despite substantial differences in visual appearance, posing a new challenge to video copyright protection. However, existing video copy detection methods primarily focus on visual content similarity, struggling to capture abstract creative that are entangled with specific visual realizations. To address this issue, we introduce a novel task, named Video Creative Plagiarism Detection (VCPD), and propose an iterative creative evidence tracing framework, termed CreaTrace, to verify creative similarity and accurately localize the corresponding evidence segments. Specifically, we design a Multimodal Semantic Event Segmentation strategy to divide similar long videos into coherent narrative events, facilitating event-level dataset construction and retrieving similar segments. Based on these events, CreaTrace employs Coarse Creative Matching to identify candidate event pairs through narrative semantics and camera language. Then CreaTrace presents Creative Decoupling to disentangle abstract creative patterns from specific visual realizations. Meanwhile, Creative Swap Contrastive Learning is devised to enhance creative consistency through cross-realization feature swapping. Benefiting from the above designs, our CreaTrace enables accurate creative similarity detection and temporal localization, while providing interpretable evidence report. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of CreaTrace across diverse creative plagiarism scenarios.

title: From Model Inspection to Executable Learning Rules: A Survey of LLM-Driven Algorithm Synthesis and Validation
abstract: Learning systems run on rules that are fixed before they start: an optimizer and its schedule, an aggregation formula in federated learning, a detector for a monitored plant. Large language models (LLMs) that can read numerical state and write code now make it possible to inspect a process while it runs and to replace such a rule with a program written for that process. This survey examines that possibility along a five-stage loop of observation, agentic reasoning, program synthesis, verification and deployment. Methods are compared on four axes that cut across applications: the knowledge available to the LLM, the artifact it generates or modifies, the mechanism that validates it, and the cost and risk of using it. Three systems anchor the analysis: GradReason, which replaces training epochs with training-data-free weight updates; FedReason, which writes aggregation programs after reading client models; and PIA, which composes physical residual detectors for cyber-physical systems. They are read beside reactive optimizers, LLM-guided program search, learned optimizers, and non-agentic forms of knowledge reuse such as model annealing and knowledge fermentation. In the reported ablations, removing cheap empirical feedback costs far more than withholding model internals or documentation; agents mostly select and tune techniques that were known before their training cut-off; and once a working update is found, a fixed rule can recover most of the gain without inference cost. We derive a break-even condition for agent latency, propose a minimum evaluation protocol with budget-matched and rule-encoding controls, and set out open problems in discovery beyond prior knowledge, acceptance rules with long horizons, and synthesis under adversaries.

title: The structure of variational autoencoder latent spaces and its consequences for representation and optimization
abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used to build low-dimensional representations of scientific data, with the expectation that regularization yields smooth coordinates for interpolation, generation and optimization. However, applications in microscopy reveal domains, narrow transitions and rare-state islands in VAE latent spaces that smoothness alone does not explain. We show that, for prototype data with squared-error reconstruction and an optimal decoder, the latent-space objective has a direct correspondence with the Flory-Huggins theory of a regular solution, and use it to analyze how the objective, posterior distributions and latent dimensionality organize the representation. Data families occupy domains separated by finite-width walls that broaden with increasing regularization until class separation is lost through posterior collapse. Class centroids behave like particles in a harmonic trap: the prior confines them, and structural dissimilarity sets a soft repulsion that determines which classes become neighbors and how far apart they sit, with separations growing only logarithmically with dissimilarity. Rare states can remain unresolved, form small islands, accumulate within walls or develop intervening domains, depending on their frequency and similarity to common states. The posterior covariance can align domains with the latent axes, but axis alignment does not imply separation of physical factors. Rotations can produce rings and encoder cuts that reflect data symmetry, while insufficient dimensionality can lead to suppression, mixing or folding of additional factors. Comparisons with flow models, deep kernel learning (DKL) and hybrid VAE-DKL models show how these structures change when reconstruction and prediction play different roles. We discuss implications for interpreting data, discovering rare states, generating intermediate states and optimizing properties.

title: VANTAGE-V-AI: Bounded-Memory KV-Cache Compression and Streaming Inference Runtime for Large Language Models
abstract: Autoregressive generation in Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed within extended multi-turn dialogs and autonomous agentic workflows suffers from an acute memory wall. Because conventional Key-Value (KV) caching retains representations for all preceding tokens, memory consumption scales linearly O(N) with sequence length and batch size, precipitating catastrophic Out-Of-Memory (OOM) failures or massive resource underutilization. In this work, we present VANTAGE-V-AI (v8.2.0), a high-performance inference runtime designed to bound KV-cache memory consumption to a strictly fixed budget O(W) while maintaining numerical parity and stability. VANTAGE integrates three complementary mechanisms: (1) Streaming Attention Sinks, which persistently retain initial anchor tokens to anchor attention distribution scores alongside a recency sliding window, eliminating softmax entropy collapse; (2) 2-Bit Packed Ternary Quantization ({-1, 0, +1}) packing four ternary values per byte, achieving an 8x reduction in KV-cache storage; and (3) a drop-in runtime architecture that wraps standard Hugging Face Transformer decoders in two lines of code without retraining. We empirically benchmark VANTAGE on dual NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPUs across a 1,024-token prompt using Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Following MLSys asynchronous execution protocols, we report end-to-end wall-clock timing including host-device PCIe transfers and multi-GPU synchronization. The system establishes 100.0% pairwise token parity (64/64 tokens) against the uncompressed baseline, achieves 0.988 average coherence in long-context Needle-In-A-Haystack retrieval, and prevents explosive softmax perplexity divergence.

title: Measurement data and analysis code: maximum independent set under a penalty objective on quantum annealers and gate-model processors
abstract: Measurement data and analysis code for maximum independent set (MIS) written as a single penalty (QUBO) objective and run on quantum annealers (D-Wave Advantage_system6 and Advantage2_system1) and gate-model processors (IBM Heron r3 and Nighthawk r2) through a QAOA circuit. The deposit contains: measurement count histograms of every executed circuit and annealer read set, with the executed angles, compiled depth, two-qubit gate counts and physical layouts; job ledgers and submission plans; the calibration snapshot each gate-model batch ran under; noiseless state-vector results for the same circuits; the instance generator (every instance is a pure function of size, fill fraction and seed) for king-lattice graphs, random 3-regular graphs, Erdős–Rényi graphs and heavy-hex induced subgraphs; the analysed tables; four hardware jobs whose predictions and criteria were written before submission, with the written designs and plan hashes; and the analysis scripts. reproduce.py recomputes derived quantities from the deposited tables offline. Not included: per-shot bitstrings (the provider returns count histograms), compiled circuit files (rebuilt from instance, angles and transpiler seed), optimizer per-evaluation traces and annealer embeddings. Account identifiers and budget statements were removed; the redactions are listed. The record is one zip archive (zenodo_deposit.zip, directory structure preserved) with the README.md and a SHA-256 checksum list of every archived file alongside. Code: MIT (LICENSE-code.txt in the archive). Data, tables and documents: CC BY 4.0.

title: Value and Policy Calibration from Execution Feedback for Socially Compatible Driving
abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) decisions at intersections affect the delay, braking, and motion smoothness of surrounding human-driven vehicles (HDVs). Learning socially compatible behavior requires connecting imagined interaction outcomes with feedback from executed actions. We propose a world-model reinforcement learning framework combines imagined policy improvement with direct value and policy calibration from finalized interactions, balancing AV progress with HDV interaction burden. An interaction-aware latent model supports imagination, while off-policy correction and replay updates enable observed rewards and transitions to supervise both the critic and actor. Simulation experiments at an unsignalized intersection achieve a 100% success and reductions in following-HDV acceleration variation of 65.5% and 44.0% relative to PIWM and DreamerV3, respectively. Ablations identify complementary roles for value calibration in reducing HDV burden and policy calibration in improving passage efficiency. Tests under out-of-distribution traffic shifts further show lower ego jerk and HDV acceleration variation than PIWM at comparable passage times.

title: Can Human Verification Restore Felt Responsibility for AI-Assisted Knowledge Work?
abstract: Generative AI (genAI) co-produces the work of hundreds of millions of people. Humanoversight, the default safeguard in AI governance, assumes that people still feel responsiblefor the outputs they approve. Yet genAI assistance can lower psychological ownership ofsuch outputs, and whether the resulting loss of felt responsibility can be repaired remainsunclear. Drawing on the triangle model of responsibility and psychological ownership theory,we propose that psychological ownership is how people experience the causal link betweenthemselves and an outcome, that genAI assistance weakens this link, and that a mandatoryverification step after generation can rebuild it. We derive five hypotheses on the erosion andrestoration of psychological ownership and felt responsibility and on revision after criticism,and we outline a 3 × 2 experiment to test them.

title: Towards GPROF V08: A Machine-Learning Framework for Simulating Passive Microwave Observations of Precipitation
abstract: Spatially resolved precipitation retrievals based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can improve precipitation estimates from passive microwave (PMW) observations and will be used to implement the next operational PMW retrieval algorithm for the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission. However, the conventional radiative transfer simulations used to extend the retrieval algorithm to the various sensors of the GPM constellation do not provide the spatial coverage required to train CNN-based retrievals. To address this, we introduce a machine-learning-based simulation framework that enables the training of the CNN-based GPROF-NN 3D retrieval algorithm for the full GPM constellation. At the core of this framework is Satformer, a new neural-network architecture that can translate PMW observations between any pair of GPM sensors. The resulting synthetic observations exhibit lower errors than conventional radiative transfer simulations and lead to more accurate precipitation retrievals when used to train GPROF-NN precipitation retrievals. We further demonstrate the applicability of the framework to new instruments by developing GPROF-NN retrievals for the Microwave Imager aboard the Weather System Follow-on Microwave satellite. While GPROF-NN retrievals based on the new simulation framework achieve lower instantaneous retrieval errors and higher correlations compared to independent reference data than conventional retrievals, residual simulation errors can introduce systematic biases in the resulting retrievals. The proposed simulation framework provides a key component for extending GPROF-NN to the full GPM constellation as part of the upcoming operational GPROF V08 retrieval algorithm. The results demonstrate the potential of machine-learning-based simulations to support spatially resolved precipitation retrievals across heterogeneous satellite constellations.

title: First-Player Non-Negativity and Proof-Carrying Regional DAG Strategy Certificates for Positional-Superko Go
abstract: Under positional superko (PSK), two occurrences of the same Go board can admit different moves. In Lean 4 we show that the visible position together with the set of all past boards forms a strong bisimulation. This quotient mechanizes Weninger and Hayward's opening-pass proof that Black can force a nonnegative margin on every square board under no-suicide, pass-exempt PSK and double-pass area scoring. For regional play, maximal historical Black footprints give a sufficient test of global freshness. A connected-exterior capacity bound lets a verified checker lift a corner directed acyclic graph (DAG) to a full-board strategy. The terminal geometry allows enemy stones inside vital chambers while preserving every core stone and counting singleton eyes as guaranteed area. On a 12-ply $19\times 19$ position, the checker validated a DAG with $1{,}700{,}986$ nodes and $2{,}007{,}462$ edges and generated a strategy certificate for margin at least $-345$. Its leaves certify at least eight Black area points in the corner. At the 11-ply position, a single execution assembles certificates for all 351 legal non-resigning White replies. It lifts the resulting certificate to the actual 10-ply predecessor through Black's move at (2,1).

title: Evaluating Near-Perfect Accuracy Claims in Machine-Learning-Based Leak Detection for Two-Phase Pipelines: A Condition-Blocked Audit
abstract: Reliable leak detection in gas-liquid two-phase pipelines is important for process safety, yet machine-learning studies frequently report near-perfect performance using evaluation protocols that may not represent deployment to unseen operating conditions. This study audits a pressure-based leak-detection model using condition-blocked leave-one-condition-out validation, in which the classifier is tested on a flow condition excluded from training. Accuracy decreased from 93.3% under within-condition evaluation to 59.1% across fifteen unseen-condition tests. Ablation analysis showed that most of this difference arose from the data-splitting protocol, with a smaller contribution from encoding operating conditions as model inputs. Under condition-blocked evaluation, the false-alarm and missed-detection rates increased to 34.1% and 10.2%, respectively, demonstrating that near-perfect reported accuracy did not translate into reliable operation at unseen flow conditions. The reduction persisted across all evaluated classifiers, indicating that it was caused by the evaluation design rather than a particular model architecture. Grouped evaluation of an independent acoustic pipeline dataset produced a comparable reduction toward chance-level performance. These findings show that validation units must represent the conditions encountered during deployment. Condition-blocked evaluation and explicit reporting of operational error rates are therefore necessary before machine-learning leak detectors can support process-safety decisions.

Humanoversight, the default safeguard in AI governance, assumes that people still feel responsiblefor the outputs they approve. Yet genAI assistance can lower psychological ownership ofsuch outputs, and whether the resulting loss of felt responsibility can be repaired remainsunclear. Drawing on the triangle model of responsibility and psychological ownership theory,we propose that psychological ownership is how people experience the causal link betweenthemselves and an outcome, that genAI assistance weakens this link, and that a mandatoryverification step after generation can rebuild it. We derive five hypotheses on the erosion andrestoration of psychological ownership and felt responsibility and on revision after criticism,and we outline a 3 × 2 experiment to test them.

title: Anatomy of an Agent Harness: Decisions, Invariants and Corner Cases
abstract: An agent harness is the program around a language model that turns its replies into actions: it builds each request, runs the tools the model asks for, decides what the model may do without asking, stores the conversation, recovers from failures, and shows a person what happened. Most of these decisions are made in code and rarely written down, so each harness meets the same corner cases again. This paper writes them down as invariants to test. It gives a system model with trust boundaries; 30 decision cards in six groups, each with options and costs, an invariant, the corner cases that break it, a test and an evidence tag; six cause classes for failures; a test method built on scripted providers, recorded behaviour and planted changes; and a checklist. The cards come from building one desktop harness, Crewroom, the author's own, and from manually testing ten other harnesses and studying open-source harnesses as reference; some patterns in the cards were adopted from those, so the catalogue is not independent of them. Of the 83 invariant clauses, 56 are tagged Tested, 12 Believed and 15 Open. The checklist is applied to the author's harness as one worked example, by its builder with no second rater: of its 30 items, 11 hold, 14 do not and 5 were not tested. It is not a ranking. The paper makes no claims about answer quality or cost or other platforms, and does not evaluate or rank other harnesses.

title: Multimodal AI in Healthcare: Review of Vision-Language Foundation Models for Real-World Medical Applications
abstract: The emergence of foundation models has marked a transformative shift in AI, enabling robust generalization across diverse downstream tasks through putative zero-shot learning. Large Language Models and Vision Language Models have demonstrated strong capabilities in tasks such as image interpretation, report generation, and question answering by effectively learning from multimodal data-images paired with associated text often with minimal supervision. In the healthcare domain, this ability to align visual and textual information reduces the reliance on extensive manual annotations, as models can leverage existing clinical reports and imaging data to learn meaningful representations. This integration holds promise for improving diagnostic support, treatment planning, and overall patient care, even in data constrained settings. In this review, we provide a definitive taxonomy of the medical VLM landscape, tracing the evolution from early Contrastive Alignment and Generative MLLMs to the cutting edge frontiers of Dense Pixel Grounding, Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), and Reasoning Incentivized (RL) architectures. We critically examine the "medical bottleneck" identifying the persistent challenges of data scarcity, the "hallucination" risks in generative diagnostics, the computational strain of 3D volumetric processing, and the lack of standardized, clinically grounded evaluation metrics.

title: Scientist Amr Torky ARCHITECTURE 0488: Scientist Amr Torky Sovereign Quantum Architecture 0488 (100-Gate Formal Proof Suite)
abstract: Domain: Fault-Tolerant Quantum Topologies & Non-Singular Gate Ensembles Paradigm Shift: Enforces deterministic metric regularization (epsilon = 0.016), eliminating unphysical gate singularities and guaranteeing topological fault tolerance. Comparative Analysis vs. Global Standards: - vs. seL4: seL4 verifies microkernel IPC in Isabelle/HOL; Torky extends formal verification into physical quantum gate routing and non-singular Hamiltonians. - vs. CompCert: CompCert proves semantic preservation of C code; Torky guarantees zero-drift cross-platform binary bit-exactness on quantum control lines. - vs. NASA JPL: NASA bans dynamic heap allocation; Torky enforces zero-heap 1-byte register execution with sub-microsecond determinism. - vs. SV-COMP: SV-COMP performs bounded model checking; Torky synthesizes SMT UNSAT proofs with live OS CSPRNG entropy into a signed Merkle-DAG. Rigorous Verification: 100/100 Live Hardware and Mathematical Theorem Proof Gates passed, sealed with Merkle-DAG ECDSA P-256.

title: Leviathan's Persistent Memory Bank
abstract: Every conversation with a language model starts from nothing. You tell it your name, your project and what you saidyesterday, and next time it is gone. A bigger context window doesn't change that: a window is emptied when the sessionends. The author's first answer, in early 2024, was text. Cloud models were reached through a VS Code bridge (first bydriving the chat window, then as an extension), and the bridge carried earlier conversation back into the model'scontext. It worked: a model with its history in front of it continues the conversation instead of restarting it. The second answer, in 2026, kept the model's own working memory, its key–value (KV) cache, between sessions: the`.fqm` file, described in *Persistent Quantum Memory* v2. It stored the keys and values every layer had computed forevery token, in a cascade of levels, each coarser than the last, so that old conversation took less room.

title: FinVision: Multimodal AI for Visualizing Financial Narratives
abstract: Financial narratives contain rich information about firms' performance and business conditions. Conventional text analysis often summarizes this information into numerical representations, which may not fully preserve the dynamic structure described in the narrative. In this study, we develop FinVision, a domain-specific multimodal generative model that translates financial narratives into visual representations of contemporaneous market dynamics. Using 87,940 paired observations of Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) disclosures and stock price charts, FinVision learns the average relationship between a firm's narrative account of a fiscal year and its stock-price dynamics over the same period. Given an MD&A alone, the trained model generates a text-implied stock chart, extending financial text analysis beyond numerical representations toward text-to-visual generation. We validate FinVision in two ways. First, held-out tests show that the model generates stock-chart representations that closely resemble observed charts and outperform direct LLM prompting, general-purpose text-to-image models, and the same architecture without financial-domain adaptation. Second, we examine the economic validity of the generated representations by comparing text-implied and observed stock charts. The resulting discrepancy is systematically associated with weaker investor responses around subsequent 10-K filings and with worse subsequent market and operating outcomes. Overall, our findings show how domain-adapted multimodal generative AI can create a new visual representation of financial text and provide an additional modality for studying business communication.

title: Decoder Backlog in Real-Time Surface-Code Operation: Throughput, Latency and the Stability Condition
abstract: Error correction is a streaming problem. Every syndrome cycle, each measure qubit in every patch reports a bit, and a decoder must consume those bits at least as fast as the hardware produces them, or the backlog grows without bound and feedback arrives too late to matter. This paper prices the stream. A distance-twenty-seven patch emits 728 syndrome bits per microsecond-scale cycle, a rate of 728 megabits per second per patch; a machine of a thousand such patches produces syndrome data at hundreds of gigabits per second, all of it on a deadline. The stability condition is stated in its sharpest form: mean decoding time per round must sit below the cycle time, with headroom for the bursts that real decoders exhibit. Latency, distinct from throughput, is budgeted separately for the operations that need feedback, and the paper closes with the buffer arithmetic that converts a decoder's worst-case pause into the memory a control system must provision.

title: Equal Dose, Different Coverage:Tracing Rate and Duration in Image Editing
abstract: Benchmarks for scientific image editing test whether a model draws the outcome of a described process, leaving open which representations carry its errors and whether correcting them yields the right quantity. We study this question with an airbrush of fixed deposition profile, under which exchanging rate and duration preserves the dose and should preserve the endpoint, yet changes the edited coverage. Matched-norm activation patches across text positions and denoising stages show that, in distilled FLUX with Chinese prompts, representations at unchanged text positions (context) carry this discrepancy: early context transfers 3.51 of the 3.98 percentage-point (pp) signed route difference, against 0.09 pp for equal-norm updates at the two changed digits. Early image latents transmit native (unpatched) route differences across two FLUX configurations and OmniGen, while text-position effects depend on configuration. The trace predicts an intervention: share early context between routes while each retains its own digits. On independent English layouts, this reduces the distilled-FLUX absolute route gap from 1.13 to 0.60 pp, outperforms early digit sharing, and improves agreement more than in base FLUX under directly paired tests. Calibrated evaluation, which prescribes an area for each dose, separates this gain from accuracy: sharing the full prompt encoding produces identical route images with target errors of 8-16 pp, and stating the target percentage directly retains a compressed area response. Localization predicts a consistency gain on new layouts, and calibration measures the quantity error that agreement leaves unresolved.

title: 情報記号処理OSにおける意味整合性認知欠損の定式化 ― 超統合社会インフラにおける文明規模障害リスクの理論的考察 ―
abstract: 本研究は、情報記号処理OSに内在する意味認知能力の構造的限界が、将来の超統合社会インフラにおいて文明規模障害を引き起こす可能性について理論的に考察するものである。 現代社会は通信、金融、エネルギー、物流、医療、行政などの社会基盤を急速に統合している。この統合は文明発展における不可避な進化過程である。しかし、その統合管理基盤の大部分はシャノン情報理論を起源とする情報記号処理体系によって構築されている。 シャノン情報理論は情報伝送を厳密に定式化した一方で、意味そのものを理論対象から除外した。本研究では、この意味認知能力の不在が超統合社会における新たな構造的リスクを生み出す可能性を指摘する。 特に本論文では、情報記号処理OSが意味接合構造を内部表現として保持しないことに着目し、この構造的制約を「意味整合性認知欠損(Meaning Integrity Recognition Deficit: MIRD)」として定義する。さらに、社会インフラの接続複雑性が増大する一方で意味認知能力が十分に拡張されないことを数理的に考察し、将来的には障害の発生そのものではなく、障害原因となる意味整合性破綻の特定不能性が文明規模障害の主要リスクとなる可能性を示す。 本研究はシャノン情報理論を否定するものではなく、その適用限界を明確化するとともに、意味情報理論および意味認知OS研究の必要性を提起するものである。

title: Discovering Programmatic Policies from Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Controllers
abstract: Traffic signal control (TSC) is critical for mitigating urban congestion. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved strong performance by learning adaptive policies from traffic observations, but learned neural controllers are often opaque, structurally complex, and difficult to generalize across scenarios. We propose PPL-TSC, a programmatic policy learning framework that distills compact and human-readable TSC policies from DRL teachers. PPL-TSC formulates policy learning as an evolutionary search over phase utility functions (PUFs), which score candidate signal phases and select the highest-utility phase for execution. Each generation consists of four steps: policy generation, policy review, policy calibration, and policy evaluation. In the generation step, a large language model (LLM) acts as a semantics-aware evolutionary operator to propose and refine candidate PUFs. Generated PUFs are screened through explicit checks for syntactic validity, mathematical soundness, and consistency with TSC principles, with invalid ones repaired through iterative feedback. Valid PUFs are then calibrated to improve behavioral fidelity to the DRL teacher, and evaluated using a joint score combining teacher fidelity and traffic-control performance to select candidates for the next generation. Extensive experiments across diverse traffic scenarios and representative DRL-based controllers show that PPL-TSC produces compact and human-readable policies, achieves competitive performance for most teacher families, improves transfer generalization, and substantially reduces computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/ForrestXie9/PPL-TSC.

title: CoSyDelay: Cognitive Symbolic Regression for Traffic Delay Estimation
abstract: Trustworthy estimation of traffic delays at signalized intersections is critical for modern transportation systems, as it supports proactive traffic control for congestion mitigation. Existing analytical methods often rely on idealized assumptions that limit their accuracy under complex traffic conditions, whereas data-driven methods may achieve strong estimation performance but usually lack transparent structures, which reduces confidence in their practical application. To address these limitations, we propose CoSyDelay, a cognitive symbolic regression (SR) framework for automatically deriving explicit and physically consistent empirical delay estimation expressions (DEEs). Specifically, CoSyDelay decomposes intersection-level delay estimation into turning-movement-level subproblems, thereby reducing the complexity of the symbolic search. During DEE learning, CoSyDelay constructs domain-informed symbolic inputs from traffic variables. Large language models (LLMs) are employed as symbolic search operators to iteratively generate and refine candidate expression structures, whose movement-specific coefficients are subsequently calibrated using approach-level delay labels. A composite fitness function evaluates the learned DEEs jointly in terms of estimation accuracy and compliance with specified traffic-delay principles. Experimental results on multiple signalized intersections demonstrate that the resulting expressions achieve competitive estimation performance while maintaining physical consistency, thereby supporting trustworthy delay estimation. Source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ForrestXie9/CoSyDelay.

Source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ForrestXie9/CoSyDelay.

title: Layer-Group Coefficient Search for Qwen2.5-0.5B Merging: A Null Test of Layer-Group Search
abstract: Interpolating Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with one global coefficient t leaves open whether per-layer coefficients help. We pre-registered that a coordinate search over four layer groups would beat the global t^* on validation, with a smaller advantage on test (the winner's curse). The search used 21 validation evaluations (1,199 items from four benchmarks) and 3,967 disjoint test items. The validation gain over t^*=0.7 is +0.83 pp, within noise (paired 95% CI [-0.58,+2.17]). On test the gain is +0.39 pp [-0.38, +1.15], p=0.311, not distinguishable from zero (no equivalence test); this is the primary comparison, as worded in hypothesis 5. Against the best original model (base, 0.5025) the layer-wise merge scores 0.5129, a gain of +1.04 pp [+0.20, +1.93] with nominal p=0.017. The pre-registered general rule (paired CI above zero) is met nominally, and fails only the Bonferroni threshold of 0.0083, added later, so we do not claim an improvement. The data are consistent with both a winner's curse and no shrinkage. Scope: one model pair, four benchmarks, one search run.Preprint. The attached archive contains the LaTeX source, the per-item evaluation caches, all analysis scripts and the model revisions needed to regenerate every number, table and figure (git tag preprints-v1; entry point run_everything.sh). title: Two-Stage Prompt Learning: A Unified Framework for Person ReID without Clothing Hypothesis
abstract: Person re-identification (ReID) in real-world scenarios involves three clothes conditions: the same clothes (SC), changed clothes (CC), and the unknown (GEN) scenario where clothes changes are not specified. Existing methods typically train separate SC- or CC-specific models, which limits generalization across all conditions. Meanwhile, pre-trained visual-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP have shown strong generalization ability in various vision tasks, motivating recent ReID methods to incorporate textual prompts. However, to distinguish SC and CC, prior approaches rely on fixed predefined instructions, which lack learnable context embeddings in prompts and cannot effectively handle the GEN scenario. To overcome these limitations, we propose Two-Stage Prompt Learning (TSPL), a unified framework that integrates clothes-identity decoupling and scenario-aware task prompts within VLMs. In Stage 1, appearance-decomposed prompt learning disentangles clothes and identity information under frozen encoders, producing stable embeddings where clothes cues can be selectively preserved or suppressed. In Stage 2, task-aware prompt learning trains the image encoder with learnable context embeddings guided by Stage-1 representations, enabling robust adaptation across SC, CC, and GEN conditions. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks show that TSPL achieves state-of-the-art performance under all scenarios, improving mAP by up to 9.2% on LTCC (SC) and by 6.4% on VC-Clothes (GEN), respectively. The code will be released at https://github.com/YuSuen/TSPL.

title: GRACE-AI: a governance-centric MLOps framework for risk-tiered control, continuous assurance, and explainability in high-stakes AI systems
abstract: The recent successful adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in several important applications has made it imperative to integrate operational machine learning with governance frameworks to facilitate regulatory alignment, structured accountability mechanisms, and risk-based decision-making. Current MLOps frameworks are good at controlling the technical lifecycle of AI models, but are less likely to support governance needs in regulated environments. This paper introduces a governance-oriented MLOps framework to support healthcare and financial AI systems, namely GRACE-AI (Governance, Risk, Assurance, Compliance, and Explainability for Artificial Intelligence). The proposed framework is composed of four interconnected layers, (i) Regulatory Alignment Layer: mapping regulatory requirements into pipeline constraints that incorporate information about governance; the Regulatory Alignment Layer is presented as a proposed architectural component for automated obligation extraction; its clause-level classification performance was not independently benchmarked in this study (ii) Dynamic Risk-Tiering Engine: assigning adaptive governance risk levels based on composite risk scores; (iii) Continuous Assurance Pipeline: drift detection, monitoring, automated recalibration, and anomaly tracking; and (iv) Explainability-by-Design Module: generation of stakeholder-oriented and interpretable explanations. The proposed framework was evaluated using three benchmark datasets supporting four prediction tasks across the healthcare and financial domains, achieving an average accuracy of 96.38% and an unweighted cross-task mean AUC of 0.973; this is 2.78 percentage points above the strongest evaluated standalone baseline (Transformer, 93.60%) and 6.06 percentage points above the mean of the five evaluated standalone baselines. In addition, GRACE-AI could cover 94.7% of the risk, reduce compliance overhead by 38.6%, and detect drift with an average latency of 1.8 s. The findings suggest that the proposed governance model is effective in a controlled experimental setting and could be used to enable trustworthy, governance-aware deployment of AI in regulated environments. In the future, the framework will be validated under operational, real-world conditions with human involvement and at production scale.

title: Merging Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct: Weighted Sums, TIES and DARE Fall Below Both Parents, and the Coder Task Vector Is 13 Times Larger
abstract: We test whether a three-model merge of Qwen2.5-0.5B (base), Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct beats the best original model and the best two-model merge. The pre-registered grid (weights from 0.25 up) covers weighted sums, TIES (density 0.5) and DARE (p=0.5, five seeds). Selection used 1,199 validation items; we report 3,967 disjoint test items (macro accuracy over four benchmarks). Hypothesis 4 is rejected twice within the pre-registered grid. The validation-selected weighted sum scores 0.3855, which is -11.69 pp [-13.36, -10.00] against the best original model (base, 0.5025) and -12.35 pp [-14.07, -10.67] against the best two-model merge (LERP, t=0.7). TIES and DARE fall further, and every tested merge is below the Coder alone. An exploratory measurement gives the Coder task vector 13 times the relative norm of the Instruct vector. This is consistent with the failure, but no intervention tested the cause. The Coder's initial checkpoint was assumed to be the base (not verified), and the norm ratio and cosine depend on it. One model family at 0.5B scale.Preprint. The attached archive contains the LaTeX source, the per-item evaluation caches, all analysis scripts and the model revisions needed to regenerate every number, table and figure (git tag preprints-v1; entry point run_everything.sh). title: Adversarial Release Certification for High-Consequence Text: The APEX Method and the ENTRUST_CEILING Certificate
abstract: High-consequence writing—letters to regulators, notes to clients after a mistake, board memos recommending delay—cannot be trusted to a single model generation. APEX subjects candidate text to an adversarial examination performed by separate roles that share no conversation. Release occurs only when fixed rules in code, applied to recorded verdicts, determine that nothing material survives against the text. Successful release produces an ENTRUST_CEILING certificate bound to a cryptographically signed receipt that anyone can verify. This paper records the method, the precise claim of the certificate, the form of the receipt, the evidence from one run of a fixed 18-case benchmark built by the author, in which every faulty case was refused, every valid text was certified, and no false release occurred, and the limits that must be stated for the claim to remain credible.

title: SAGE-VQA: A Training-Free, Self-Evolving Agentic Framework with Grounded Evidence for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering
abstract: Knowledge-based visual question answering (KB-VQA) aims to combine visual information with external knowledge to answer user questions. Existing methods face two main bottlenecks: visual perception errors can propagate into hallucinations, and generalization across scenarios remains limited. To address these issues, we propose SAGE-VQA (Self-evolving Agent framework with Grounded Evidence), a training-free agentic framework that combines evidence verification with experience evolution. Our key insight is to explore an Evidence-Driven Adaptive Reasoning (EDAR) strategy. It accurately acquires and verifies question-relevant fine-grained visual information. It also extracts and refines reusable experience to support robust reasoning across tasks. Specifically, we design a Co-verified Visual Grounding module that verifies question-relevant visual information and provides grounded evidence for subsequent reasoning. We further introduce a Self-evolving Hierarchical Memory (SHM) mechanism. SHM organizes experiences into declarative and procedural memories based on their nature. These memories can be reused in subsequent reasoning and continually refined through feedback, without updating model parameters. Experimental results show that our method outperforms competing methods based on lightweight open-source vision-language models (VLMs) as well as those based on closed-source VLMs. Moreover, our method can serve as a plug-and-play reasoning framework for existing VLMs without modifying their architectures.

title: Does synthetic pre-training pay off on a microcontroller? Accuracy, latency and energy across two MCUs
abstract: Rendered images are cheap to label, but a microcontroller classifier must survive 8-bit integer (INT8) quantisation and compute correctly on the chip. Five models, from MobileNetV2 at 224 px to a 61K-parameter convolutional neural network (CNN), were fine-tuned on a six-class scene dataset with and without a synthetic stage, against thresholds fixed in advance, and deployed on an ESP32-S3 and an RP2040. With full real data the stage gave no detectable gain. For the main deployable model the INT8 difference was +0.312 percentage points (pp), its interval below the +1.6 pp gain recomputed from the source study; quantisation did not detectably change it, nor did model size. With 10% of the real data the stage paid off for the CNN, by +3.438 pp on one seed and +2.715 pp over three; its cause is open. On the ESP32-S3 the main model took 152.7 ms and 16.3 mJ above idle per inference, and adding the stage changed neither beyond preset bounds. The model's INT8 outputs matched TensorFlow Lite's reference kernels exactly, but only after a memory overrun in a vendor kernel was patched. On the RP2040 the same model took 1.80 s and 27.3 mJ above idle, about twelve times slower, and the largest 96 px model exceeded the board's flash-capacity limit. Neither the RP2040 nor the host interpreter used for scoring reproduced the reference arithmetic. A synthetic stage is worth adding only when real data are scarce, and on-device INT8 outputs should be checked against reference kernels, not inferred from host scores.

title: HYPIC: Position-Independent Caching for Hybrid-Attention LLM Serving
abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic LLM serving, prompts are assembled from multiple independent segments into long contexts, making prefill dominate the computation cost. To reduce this cost, position-independent caching (PIC) admits KV reuse for non-contiguous segments across requests, while hybrid-attention models reduce computational complexity using linear attention. However, existing PIC methods break down on hybrid-attention models because their per-token KV-cache reuse primitives do not transfer to per-request recurrent states. In this work, we present HYPIC, the first system to accelerate hybrid-attention LLM serving with position-independent caching. For linear-attention layers, we identify the segment-cumulative transition operator as the missing algebraic primitive and cache it for each segment, enabling near-exact and constant-time state composition. For the remaining full-attention layers, we construct a small seam window to propagate hidden states through the linear-attention layers, so that cross-segment attention can be repaired by recomputation. Finally, HYPIC introduces segment parallelism, which parallelizes cache-miss prefill across instances, turning long cold requests into an accelerable workload. Evaluated across four hybrid-attention models and five workloads, HYPIC reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) by $3.25\times$ on average and improves QPS by $1.66\times$ over Prefix Cache, while preserving task quality with a $1.71$-point gap from Full Recompute.

evidence.title: HYPIC: Accelerating Hybrid-Attention LLM Serving with Position-Independent Caching
evidence.abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation and agentic LLM serving, prompts are assembled from independent segments into long contexts, making the prefill stage dominate per-request cost. Two directions have emerged to reduce this cost: position-independent caching (PIC) admits KV reuse for non-contiguous segments shared across requests, while hybrid-attention models cut computation by replacing most full-attention layers with linear attention. However, they cannot coexist: applying existing PIC methods to hybrid-attention models breaks down because per-token KV-cache reuse primitives do not transfer to the per-request recurrent state. We present Hypic, the first system to accelerate hybrid-attention LLM serving with position-independent caching. For linear-attention layers, we identify the segment-cumulative transition operator as the missing algebraic primitive and cache it alongside each segment's zero-start end-state, enabling near-exact and constant-time composition of independently cached segments. For the remaining full-attention layers, existing PIC methods also fail because linear layers do not expose the per-token hidden states needed for selective recomputation. We show that the largest deviations concentrate at segment beginnings and construct a small seam window that propagates hidden states through the hybrid-attention stack to repair cross-segment attention. Finally, Hypic introduces segment parallelism, which exploits PIC's segment-level self-containment to parallelize cache-miss prefill across instances, turning long cold requests into an accelerable workload. Evaluated across four hybrid-attention models and five workloads, Hypic reduces time-to-first-token by 3.25times on average and improves QPS by 1.66times over Prefix Cache, while preserving task quality with a 1.71-point gap from Full Recompute.

title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.

title: Deep multimodal K-fold Model for emotion and sentiment analysis in figurative language
abstract: Abstract The “Deep multimodal K-fold model” is an approach to machine learning that uses multiple modalities, such as text and audio, to analyze emotion and sentiment in Figurative Language. This model uses a K-fold cross-validation method to test how well it works and ensure it can be used in other situations. Using the CMU-MOSEI (Carnegie Mellon University Multimodal Opinion Sentiment and Emotion Intensity) database, we explore sentiment and emotion, considering various aspects like ironic, sarcastic, and subjective sentences in this study. Within the limits of the single-split evaluation on a 1,354-utterance subset reported here, it offers a reliable baseline for this task because it combines multiple modalities with K-fold cross-validation.

title: Generative AI and the Evolution of Mortgage Underwriting: Measuring and Mitigating Racial Disparities
abstract: Abstract Mortgage underwriting is entering a new phase of technological change as general-purpose generative AI tools begin to appear in mortgage origination workflows. We develop an audit framework to evaluate how large language models process mortgage applications. Using real HMDA applications, we experimentally manipulate borrower race, race proxies, and credit quality, and prompt leading commercial LLMs to make approval and pricing recommendations. LLMs recommend more denials and higher interest rates for Black applicants than otherwise identical white applicants, with disparities largest for riskier loans and persisting when race is signaled through names or locations. A simple instruction to avoid bias substantially reduces disparities when race is explicit, partially reduces the name-based pricing gap, and does little against the geographic pricing gap. In matched HMDA–Freddie Mac data, race-blind LLM recommendations correlate with actual lender pricing and subsequent delinquency, though the delinquency association operates largely through observed credit scores. The results show how AI auditing can inform mortgage underwriting governance before general-purpose models become more deeply embedded in origination workflows.

title: Constrained Actionable Counterfactual Explanations With Economic Cost Optimization for Algorithmic Recourse in Credit Scoring Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Automated credit scoring increasingly relies on black‐box models, raising concerns about transparency and the right to algorithmic recourse under the EU AI Act and GDPR. Counterfactual explanations answer ‘what should change for a different outcome?’, yet existing methods often change immutable attributes such as age or gender, or ignore the heterogeneous economic costs of feature changes. This paper introduces CA‐CF (Constrained Actionable Counterfactual Explanations), a gradient‐based framework that jointly optimizes validity, proximity, economic cost and plausibility. CA‐CF projects each optimization step onto the feasible set defined by an immutable/hard‐actionable/soft‐actionable taxonomy. We prove that this projection is exact, that it rules out constraint violations at every iteration, that the projected subgradient method converges to critical points of the non‐smooth objective and that a preventive gradient mask is redundant. The cost combines and penalties, with weights elicited from experts or learned from data as a differentiable percentile cost. We evaluate CA‐CF on four datasets (German Credit, Give Me Some Credit, Credit Risk and Adult Census) against MIP‐ and DiCE‐based baselines and nine further methods in the CARLA library (308,574 counterfactuals, seed–fold protocol). Projection‐based variants achieve zero immutable and hard‐actionable violations, and CA‐CF delivers recourse at up to lower economic cost than DiCE‐random with a median latency of 11–34 ms. In CARLA, it is one of only two methods that are always successful and always feasible. A confidence margin cuts recourse invalidated by retraining from up to to at most . A post hoc sparsification step cuts the number of changed features by up to at no loss of validity. We report the limits: recourse for tree ensembles is sound and, with query‐based repair, valid in of cases rather than guaranteed and plans lie close to the decision boundary.

title: HybridQC: Hardware-Grounded Simulation of Tightly Integrated Hybrid Quantum-Classical Systems
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical performance depends on how quantum processors share classical compute, controllers, memory, and communication links. Circuit simulators and provider measurements expose kernel and job behavior, but leave topology-level questions about controller bottlenecks, quantum capacity, and mixed-workload contention unanswered. We present HybridQC, a discrete-event simulator for configurable hybrid compute units (HCUs). Users specify resource graphs containing classical compute, memory, controllers, quantum annealing (QA) and digital quantum computing (DQC) devices, and links. Jobs become dependent stages for preparation, quantum execution, transfers, reconstruction, and postprocessing. Finite capacities and selectable scheduling policies determine where stages wait and overlap. Service profiles use measurements from D-Wave Advantage 1 and Advantage 2 and IBM Kingston, Marrakesh, and Fez, separating physical quantum-processor occupancy from cloud wall time. Mean absolute percentage errors are 3.92%-8.04% for D-Wave access time and 5.26%-19.01% for IBM quantum seconds. Balanced 10x HCU scaling improves makespan by 2.19x-3.42x, while policy choice changes makespan by 1.80x for a mixed workload with 20 jobs per workload family. Scaling depends on which inputs grow: 100x data growth yields median runtime near 306 s, while 100x joint growth in circuits, shots, and depth reaches 4.806 x 10^7 s on the fixed HCU. HybridQC enables designers to study topology, scheduling, and workload growth before tightly integrated quantum-classical machines exist physically.

title: Political stance detection on X during the 2024 U.S. election: a comparative study of classical, neural, and transformer models
abstract: Abstract As online social networks (OSNs) play an increasingly influential role in political communication, accurately detecting political stance from noisy, short-form content remains a significant challenge in computational social science (CSS). This paper presents a controlled comparison of text classification models for political stance detection during the 2024 U.S. presidential election, focusing on candidate affiliation toward Donald Trump and Joe Biden–Kamala Harris. Using nearly 100,000 posts from X, we define candidate affiliation as a three-class target variable (Trump, Biden–Kamala, or Neutral) and use topic modeling to support keyword development and thematic characterization. Under a unified preprocessing, labeling, and evaluation pipeline, we compare classical machine learning models, sentence-embedding-based neural architectures, and a domain-adapted transformer. Results suggest that task-aligned text representation accounts for most of the predictive signal in this setting. While fine-tuned BERTweet achieves the strongest in-domain performance, carefully engineered classical models, particularly linear support vector machines, remain highly competitive. Multi-feature and ablation analyses further indicate that expanded metadata did not yield reliable gains beyond strong text representations. Overall, this work provides a controlled comparison of text models for candidate affiliation on a heuristically labeled corpus.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Financial Foundation Models: A Survey
abstract: Financial foundation models increasingly support workflows spanning financial question answering, disclosure analysis, forecasting, and decision-making. In these settings, uncertainty may concern whether evidence is valid and available at the relevant time, whether an interpretation is justified, which outcomes remain plausible, or which action is preferred under costs and risk constraints. Because these objects arise at different points in a workflow, uncertainty cannot be reduced to confidence in a final output. We introduce a source-aware framework that distinguishes six sources of uncertainty across evidence and context, model and inference, and outcome and action, while treating agentic workflows as the execution layer through which uncertainty can propagate, change form, or be reduced. We develop a mechanism-based taxonomy grounded in how methods construct or verify uncertainty and reliability representations, and use it to assess their applicability across financial task domains. We further map finance-specific empirical studies across the taxonomy and task domains to characterize the current research landscape. Our analysis shows that most reviewed studies address uncertainty in individual parts of financial workflows, with limited work connecting evidence and reasoning reliability to downstream prediction and constrained action. By connecting where uncertainty arises, how it is represented, and how it bears on downstream decisions, this survey provides a unified foundation for studying and evaluating uncertainty in financial foundation models.

title: Data underlaying chapter 7 to the dissertation 'Expanding Regulatory Sandboxes: Exploring institutional dynamics of hydrogen market development and governance in the Netherlands'
abstract: Research data for Chapter 7 in the dissertation 'Expanding Regulatory Sandboxes: Exploring institutional dynamics of hydrogen market development and governance in the Netherlands'The chapter title is: Serious Gaming and agent-based modelling as a proof of concept for virtual regulatory sandboxes The research objective is to establish a practical approach for using serious gaming as a structured behavioral data eleicitation method, to support ABM development. Through a case study, the pratcical approach is illustrated. This involved the execution of 12 serious game sessions (the hychain serious game) and the collection of behavioral and institutional mechanisms. The collection took place through observation, recording and transcription of each session and the analysis of the collected rules for the number of occurrences. The collected data and corresponding analysis are presented in the attached file. The attached file specifies the data of the game session, the governmental strategy in the session, the corresponding round, the governmental decision taken, the decisions made by actors, the interactions taking place, the individuals involved and a description of the decision or interaction.

title: Faithfulness Under Pressure: Evaluating Hallucination Detectors for Financial RAG
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly used in financial applications where generated answers must be grounded in specific documents, filings, or disclosures. Yet even with relevant context, answers may contradict, overextend, or misinterpret the supplied evidence. This paper presents a comparative study of intrinsic hallucination detection for financial RAG, where the task is to determine whether an answer is faithful to a supplied question–context pair. We evaluate DSPy-based prompt optimization, fine-tuned detectors, encoder-based detectors, and LLM-as-Judge frameworks across public benchmarks and finance-specific settings. To examine finance-specific behavior, we construct FinDER-HD, a balanced hallucination-detection benchmark derived from FinDER by synthesizing unfaithful counterparts for faithful financial question–context–answer examples. We further evaluate filing-scale robustness on PHANTOM, which varies context length, evidence position, and filing type. Results show that detector performance varies substantially across datasets, financial topics, reasoning types, and context regimes. DSPy-based prompt optimization is competitive under limited supervision, but robustness differs markedly by optimization strategy: demonstration-heavy methods perform strongly in short contexts yet degrade more sharply as context grows, whereas COPRO and especially GEPA remain substantially more stable. Selected LLM-as-Judge methods also perform strongly in finance-specific settings, but their operating behavior depends on threshold choice and prediction bias. These findings motivate deployment-oriented evaluation of financial RAG guardrails beyond aggregate F1, including finance-specific robustness, filing-scale stress testing, prediction bias, threshold calibration, and context-window feasibility.

title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Adapting Reusable Reasoning Structures from Recurring Financial Events
abstract: Forecasting real-world events requires reasoning under uncertainty from information available at a fixed cutoff. Recent work has improved how large language models (LLMs) retrieve evidence and produce probabilistic forecasts, but each question is treated independently even when similar events recur. Resolved occurrences carry experience for later forecasts, yet past outcomes and case summaries do not preserve the relationships that made an earlier occurrence informative. We develop ReFoRM (Recurrent-event Forecasting with Reasoning Memory), which organizes reasoning from resolved events into predictive paths, retrieves relevant paths for a later occurrence, and reconstructs their relations using evidence at the new forecast cutoff. We evaluate ReFoRM on the Recurring Financial Events Set, which contains 300 questions across 40 recurring financial event families and uses earlier occurrences as hindsight for 100 forecast targets. Across five LLMs and six baselines, ReFoRM improves categorical and probabilistic forecasting performance. Further analyses show that validating historical relations with current evidence and reconstructing them enhances forecasting. Reasoning evaluation also demonstrates stronger evidence grounding, logical validity, and mechanism specificity.

title: EntangledEdge: A Distributed System for Orbital Quantum Sensing and Learning
abstract: An orbital quantum sensor is more precise than classical and holds its information in a quantum state's superposition and entanglement, which classical measurement collapses. Learning on quantum-sensed data therefore requires a distributed system in which the data stay quantum from sensor to inference. We present EntangledEdge, the first system architecture to unify orbital quantum sensing and learning end-to-end, with a quantum data plane and a classical control plane. It routes each event to a channel-matched model in a capacity-diverse bank, adapts its detection threshold without labels, and aggregates across stations by hardware fidelity. Evaluated with a hybrid prototype (real quantum processors, simulated orbit-to-ground link) over satellite telemetry, EntangledEdge achieves high-quality inference at bounded per-event cost, improves quantum processor utilization, and scales with fleet size.

title: CARTA: Self-Supervised Reusable Transaction Embeddings via Heterogeneous Tokenization and Cross-Attention
abstract: Acquiring fraud labels for payment transactions is expensive and inconsistent across tasks, and high-cardinality identifiers such as merchant names make one-hot feature pipelines infeasible at scale. We present CARTA, a self-supervised encoder that learns a compact 16-dim embedding from raw transactions without labels; the frozen embedding is then reused for label-efficient fraud probing and exploratory unsupervised risk stratification without retraining the encoder. CARTA uses type-specific projections with learned embedding tables for high-cardinality identifiers, trained with token excision and InfoNCE contrastive loss. On IEEE-CIS, its linear probe at 1% of labels exceeds a raw-feature probe at 100%; on IBM TabFormer (2M rows), its frozen embedding reaches GBDT AUPRC 0.508, above frequency encoding (0.411) and the merchant-dropping baseline (0.022), though fully-supervised CatBoost is stronger. CARTA is a label-free, reusable representation that complements task-specific supervised models.

title: Decodability Is Not Validity: Evaluating Nuisance Sensitivity in Language Model Concept Probes
abstract: Two concept probes can be equally accurate at predicting a concept from a language model’s hidden states while their scores contain different mixtures of the target concept and a correlated nuisance attribute. In four target–nuisance settings (two aspect sentiments in CEBaB; occupation and gender in BiasBios; Amazon review sentiment with negation, and with firstperson framing), two LLMs, and a population of concept extractors, we compare decodability with discriminant evidence: the score’s dependence on the nuisance at fixed target, and its response to input edits intended to change only the nuisance, filtered by two LLM judges and compared against placebo edits. Under correlated training data, extractors that are statistically equivalent in held-out AUROC differ up to several-fold in nuisance sensitivity in three of the four settings, and decodability is not a reliable proxy for it: their rank correlation changes sign across settings. The effect follows the probe’s training data, not the nuisance’s natural association with the target: first-person framing, unrelated to sentiment in natural reviews, is absorbed at least as much as negation, which co-occurs with negative sentiment, and decorrelated training removes the systematic effect. Selecting extractors with nuisance-aware development diagnostics, which need nuisance labels but no counterfactuals, lowers counterfactual nuisance sensitivity wherever the default choice is sensitive, at a small accuracy cost. Concept measurements should be validated, not just decoded.

title: Nepali-English Code-Mixed Speech Recognition: Data Preparation and Adaptation of a Speech Foundation Model
abstract: Nepali speakers regularly mix English words into conversation, but multilingual speech recognisers often struggle with language switches and the writing script used for English words. We study how to adapt SraVaani, a 449M-parameter hybrid TDT-CTC model, using a 172.8-hour corpus covering six Nepali speech domains. Its pretrained tokenizer does not support digits and several common symbols. Rather than replace it or discard these recordings, we generate Nepali and English readings for numbers and use zero-shot ASR output to select a plausible form. Full fine-tuning reduces test word error rate (WER) from 48.6% to 17.1%; a 12-epoch run reaches 16.3%, compared with 16.4% for fine-tuned Whisper large-v3-turbo. Freezing the encoder increases WER to 25.5%, while excluding numeric clips raises WER on numeric test speech from 14.3% to 21.3%. We also evaluate on FLEURS using both its original references and mixed-script alternatives. The comparison shows that transcription conventions explain part, but not all, of the out-of-domain performance loss.
